prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: And, The, Still

outputs.L1:
In the dog days of summer, as muslin curls in its own heat  
And crickets cry in the black walnut tree,  
The wind lifts up my life  
And sets it some distance from where it was.

Still, Marco Polo Airport wore me out;  
I slept in a plastic chair, then took the water taxi.  
Early—too early—the voices of children  
Mimicked the clatter in the Internet café  
In Campo Santo Stefano, in a place of black coffee,  
Bordellos of verse, bony accolades of joy.

Saint Stephen stooped over a cross,  
A dog licking his heel, blood dripping from a sign  
By the church wall—*Anarchia è ordine*—  
The refugee from Istria gathers up nails.  
She will cobble together a gondola from bits of driftwood  
Cast off the shores of the hunger-bitten Adriatic.

In the wind off the lagoon,  
A child hops through numbered squares,  
Back and forth, back and forth,  
A cap on his head, rhymes cool as bone in his mouth.  
Whose child is he?  
No one will answer me.

Voices from the music academy pour into sunlight  
That strikes the malarial wealth of empire,  
Dreams of an old man in terrible heat,  
Hands bound with coarse cloth, tethered to a scaffold,  
Still painting waves on the walls of the Palazzo Ducale.
outputs.L2:
During the fiercest heat of summer, when muslin twists in the warmth it holds,  
and crickets call from the black walnut,  
a gust raises my life  
and places it away from where it had been.

Even so, Marco Polo Airport exhausted me.  
I dozed in a plastic seat  
and then boarded the water taxi.

At an hour far too early, children’s voices  
copied the rattling noise of the Internet café  
in Campo Santo Stefano,  
in a setting of dark coffee,  
brothel-like rooms of poetry,  
thin praises of happiness.

Saint Stephen bends above a cross,  
a dog lapping at his heel.  
Blood falls from a notice  
beside the church wall:  
“Anarchia è ordine.”

The woman displaced from Istria collects nails.  
With scraps of driftwood  
thrown away by the starving Adriatic’s coasts,  
she will piece together a gondola.

In the breeze coming from the lagoon,  
a boy jumps through numbered boxes,  
to and fro, again and again,  
a cap on his head,  
chants in his mouth as cold as bone.

Whose boy is this?  
No one gives me an answer.

Sounds from the music academy spill out into the daylight,  
which hits the fever-ridden riches of empire:  
the visions of an aged man in unbearable heat,  
his hands tied with rough fabric,  
fastened to a scaffold,  
still covering the walls of the Palazzo Ducale  
with painted waves.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker undergoing a disorienting summer journey, one that unsettles their ordinary sense of life, identity, and place. Travel does not simply move the speaker from one location to another; it alters perception. The experience of arriving in and moving through Venice becomes dreamlike and unstable, as if the city’s beauty and history are constantly shifting beneath the surface. The summer heat, the movement through streets and canals, and the encounter with unfamiliar scenes all contribute to a feeling of displacement.

Venice is portrayed through a series of vivid and memorable images. The poem evokes the atmosphere of travel, with its arrivals, departures, and passing impressions, as well as the social spaces of cafés, churches, and public squares. These locations create a rich sense of urban life: people gather, worship, talk, rest, observe, and pass by one another. The city appears both intimate and theatrical, full of visual detail and historical resonance. Its buildings, religious spaces, and public areas suggest a place shaped by centuries of art, power, commerce, and ritual.

At the same time, the poem does not present Venice as merely beautiful or romantic. It repeatedly contrasts pleasure and aesthetic richness with darker realities. Images of joy, music, play, and architectural splendor are set against poverty, exile, violence, and political unrest. This contrast gives the poem much of its emotional force. Venice becomes a place where beauty cannot erase suffering, and where the pleasures of travel are shadowed by awareness of social and historical pain. The speaker sees not only the city’s charm but also the instability and hardship that exist within and around it.

Children’s voices and games recur throughout the poem, adding another important layer of meaning. Their songs, cries, and play suggest innocence, vitality, and continuity. Yet these children are not placed in a secure or timeless world. Their presence occurs amid signs of historical change, social inequality, and political anxiety. As a result, their innocence feels fragile. The sound of children playing may offer moments of hope or human warmth, but it also sharpens the poem’s awareness of vulnerability and uncertainty.

The poem also reflects on Venice’s imperial past and artistic legacy. The city is associated with grandeur, cultural achievement, and historical power, but these associations are no longer uncomplicated. Its former glory is shadowed by suffering, oppressive heat, physical decay, and reminders of decline. The beauty of Venice remains undeniable, yet it is presented as haunted by the costs of history. In this way, the poem becomes not just a description of a city, but a meditation on civilization itself: how art, empire, joy, and violence can coexist in the same place, and how travel can reveal both the magnificence and the fragility of human life.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents Venice not as a stable or purely beautiful destination, but as a fractured landscape shaped by displacement, memory, and historical violence. Its structure resembles a fragmented travelogue: the speaker moves through the city in flashes, noticing streets, water, buildings, churches, crowds, and political signs without ever fully settling into them. This movement creates a sense of exhaustion and disorientation. Venice becomes a place that is seen while in transit, through a consciousness already burdened by fatigue, exile, and the pressure of history.

Throughout the poem, personal perception is inseparable from collective memory. The speaker’s tiredness is not merely physical; it suggests the deeper weariness of someone carrying historical trauma. Images of urban beauty are repeatedly shadowed by reminders of suffering. Religious symbols, architectural grandeur, and political references all point beyond the surface of the city to the violence that helped produce or preserve it. Venice’s canals, churches, and monuments may appear magnificent, but the poem insists that such magnificence cannot be separated from empire, conquest, exclusion, and loss.

The city therefore becomes haunted. Its beauty is real, but it is never innocent. The poem suggests that every image of splendor contains traces of those who were displaced, exploited, or forgotten. Venice is not simply a museum of art and history; it is a space where history continues to press upon the present. The speaker’s fragmented impressions reveal how the past survives in the details of the city, turning ordinary sights into signs of collective grief.

By blending private exhaustion with vivid urban, religious, and political imagery, the poem shows how individual experience can open onto broader historical realities. The speaker’s movement through Venice becomes a way of confronting the relationship between beauty and violence, memory and exile. In the end, the poem portrays the city as both dazzling and wounded: a place where aesthetic pleasure is inseparable from suffering, and where personal observation reveals the deeper losses hidden beneath the surface of empire.
outputs.L5:
**And, The, Still**

And the world keeps moving. The sun rises, the streets fill, voices return, and days begin again. Still, there are moments when everything feels quiet, as if time has paused just long enough for us to notice what usually passes unseen.

And in that stillness, the small things matter: the sound of rain on a window, the warmth of a familiar place, the comfort of a simple thought. The world may be busy, uncertain, and loud. Still, there is beauty in continuing, in waiting, in breathing, and in beginning once more.

And so we move forward. The path may not always be clear. Still, every step carries meaning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the style of late 20th-century American lyric poetry, set in Venice after arriving through Marco Polo Airport, mixing travel fatigue, political graffiti, children’s voices, refugees, and images of empire.
counterfactuals.output:
After Marco Polo Airport  
the bus coughs us toward water,  
past warehouses, glass weeds,  
the tired syntax of arrival—  
passport, carousel, fluorescent dawn.

My body is a country  
badly governed by sleep.  
In the windows, my face  
floats over the causeway,  
over the flat lagoon  
where the first light lifts  
like a coin from a dead emperor’s mouth.

Venice appears as rumor,  
then stone, then bruise-colored water.  
A bell opens somewhere  
and pigeons scatter  
like torn dispatches.

On a wall near the vaporetto stop  
someone has written  
NO BORDERS  
in red paint,  
and beneath it, in another hand,  
EUROPA ASSASSINA.  
The words lean into the salt air,  
urgent, almost beautiful,  
as if beauty were not always  
being asked to testify.

Children run ahead  
with wheeled suitcases,  
their voices bright as knives  
against the morning.  
One counts bridges.  
One asks if the sea is a street.  
One sings a song  
I cannot place,  
the vowels skipping  
over the stones.

At the dock, men wait  
with plastic bags,  
with phones held like small lamps,  
with the gaze of those  
who have crossed too much water  
to admire it.  
Their jackets are thin.  
The city behind them  
rises in marble and gold,  
old merchant republic,  
old hunger in a mask.

Here are the winged lions,  
the saints, the loot transfigured  
into chapel light.  
Here are the maps  
where other people’s coasts  
were made ornamental.  
Here is empire  
wearing its evening face  
at nine in the morning.

I drag my suitcase  
over the bridge’s teeth.  
Each step is an argument  
between wheels and stone.  
Sleep blooms blackly  
behind my eyes.  
The canal smells of diesel,  
algae, history refusing  
to become history.

A woman in a headscarf  
holds a child against her coat.  
The child watches the water  
as if it might explain  
how one shore becomes another,  
how a name survives  
the mouth that must speak it  
to officials.

Above us, laundry lifts  
from balconies—  
white shirts, blue sheets,  
the flags of the ordinary  
briefly sovereign.

I want to say  
the city is sinking,  
but every city is sinking  
under what it remembers  
and what it will not.  
The palaces keep their faces  
turned toward the canal.  
The graffiti keeps speaking  
from the walls.  
The children keep asking  
where we are going.

And I, newly arrived,  
salt-stung, unwashed,  
carrying my little republic  
of receipts and errors,  
stand in the broken glitter  
of the Grand Canal  
and feel the morning pass through me—

not absolution,  
not welcome,  
only light  
touching everything  
with the same indifferent hand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, literary poem that begins with “In the dog days of summer” and moves from a hot American summer image into Venice, including Campo Santo Stefano, a water taxi, anarchist graffiti, the Adriatic, and the Palazzo Ducale.
counterfactuals.output:
In the dog days of summer the asphalt sweats its tar-black psalm,  
cornfields flare like brass, cicadas stitch the noon shut,  
and porch fans turn their slow republic of dust—  
then suddenly the mind, heat-struck, crosses water: Venice,  
salt-lipped and sinking, opening her green canals  
like veins beneath a saint’s translucent skin.

In Campo Santo Stefano, evening loosens its amber hair;  
children scatter pigeons through the ocher air,  
a church bell bruises the hour, and from a wall  
anarchist graffiti blooms—black letters, quick as knives—  
against the patient stucco of centuries.

A water taxi shoulders the canal, varnished, predatory,  
its wake worrying the reflections of palaces  
into broken gold. Beyond the lagoon, the Adriatic  
breathes its blue animal breath, ancient and indifferent,  
carrying the rumor of storms, crusades, drowned emperors.

And there, the Palazzo Ducale—lace of stone,  
tyrant’s wedding cake, honeycomb of judgment—  
floats in its own mirage, while summer, American and Venetian,  
burns through one body: sun on screen doors, sun on marble,  
the same fever lifting history like a veil  
from the face of water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an ekphrastic travel poem about Venice in a melancholy, fragmented voice, with references to crickets, black walnut trees, an Internet café, Saint Stephen, Istrian refugees, children playing hopscotch, and an old painter in the Doge’s Palace.
counterfactuals.output:
**Venice, After the Painting**

In the Doge’s Palace,  
an old painter sits beneath a ceiling of thunder—  
gold saints, bruised clouds,  
the republic lifting its torn silk to the light.

His hand trembles.  
Not from age, he says,  
but from water.

Outside, Venice keeps dissolving  
into its own reflection:  
a bell, a bridge,  
a woman carrying bread through fog.

At San Stefano—Saint Stephen—  
pigeons scatter like ash.  
The stones remember knees, processions,  
the small violence of prayer.

I walk without arrival.

In a campo, children play hopscotch  
over chalk squares already fading.  
One foot in earth,  
one foot in heaven,  
their laughter strikes the walls  
and falls into the canal.

Somewhere, crickets sing  
as if there were still fields here,  
as if black walnut trees  
leaned over the lagoon,  
dropping their dark fruit  
into water green as old copper.

At the Internet café,  
blue screens glow on faces  
of boys calling home,  
tourists checking weather,  
Istrian refugees searching names  
that history misfiled—  
Pola, Fiume, Rovigno—  
each place a window left open  
in winter.

I read nothing.  
I send nothing.  
The cursor blinks,  
patient as a lighthouse.

Venice:  
you are not a city  
but a canvas left wet.

The old painter in the palace  
adds another shadow  
to a martyr’s robe.  
He does not look up  
when the tide enters the room  
in my imagination.

Crickets.  
Walnuts.  
Children’s chalk.  
Saint Stephen’s stones.

All of it drifting—  
even the gold,  
even the names,  
even the hand  
that tries to hold the scene  
still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal narrative poem about exhaustion after landing at Marco Polo Airport, wandering through Venice, overhearing children and music students, and reflecting on exile, poverty, empire, and art.
counterfactuals.output:
At Marco Polo Airport, sleep left me  
like a country revoked at the border.

The plane opened its silver mouth.  
We spilled out—tourists, widows, businessmen,  
a choir of rolling suitcases  
clicking their little teeth against the floor.

Above us, signs in three languages  
fluttered like captured birds.  
A mural of the winged lion watched  
with the patience of empire:  
one paw on the book, one paw on the sea,  
all gold leaf and threat.

I had not slept in a century.  
My eyes were two customs officers  
stamping every face with suspicion.  
My hands smelled of recycled air,  
my shirt of someone else’s weather.

Outside, the lagoon waited,  
green-black, silk-rotten, imperial.  
Boats came and went like hallucinations.  
Venice rose from the water  
not as a city but as a rumor  
poverty had polished until it shone.

I took the vaporetto with the others.  
The engine coughed up dark flowers.  
Palaces drifted past, each one  
a marble mask over a drowned mouth.  
Their windows stared at me  
with the blind elegance of old creditors.

Somewhere, under the water,  
coins were still falling—  
ducats, lire, euros, teeth.  
The sea collected them all  
and paid no one back.

At Rialto the crowds thickened.  
Selfie sticks lifted like spears.  
A child in a red jacket shouted,  
Look, Mama, the houses are sinking!  
and his mother laughed  
the way adults laugh at prophecy.

Another child asked  
if the gondoliers lived in the boats,  
if the pigeons had passports,  
if the statues were dead people  
or only very tired angels.

I wanted to answer:  
Yes.

Yes, to all of it.

The angels are exhausted.  
The statues are waiting for wages.  
The pigeons are citizens  
of every collapsing republic.

In a narrow calle  
I lost the map, then my shadow,  
then briefly my name.  
Laundry hung overhead  
like flags of surrender—  
sheets, shirts, a child’s small socks  
swaying above the stone  
as if the poor had conquered the sky  
with soap and string.

From an open window came scales:  
violin, clarinet, a piano  
stumbling up and down its ladder of notes.  
Music students, invisible,  
were practicing hunger into beauty.  
Again, again, the violin insisted,  
sawing at the same bright nerve.  
Again, again, the piano replied,  
as if art were a door  
that opened only when kicked.

Then a trumpet entered—  
golden, adolescent, wounded—  
and the whole alley widened  
into a cathedral no pope had purchased.

I stood beneath it,  
my luggage leaning against my leg  
like an obedient animal,  
and thought of exile.

Not the grand exile  
painted in museums—  
the poet with his cloak,  
the prince on the pier,  
the saint staring nobly east—

but the cheaper kind:  
the father sending wages home  
from a mattress behind a restaurant,  
the woman cleaning hotel rooms  
where the pillows are whiter  
than any official forgiveness,  
the child translating bills  
before learning the names of stars.

Exile with a plastic bag.  
Exile with bad shoes.  
Exile waiting at Western Union.  
Exile eating standing up.

Venice glittered around me,  
a jeweled wound.  
Every bridge arched its back  
like an old servant.  
Every church lifted its ceiling  
above the muttering water  
and said: Behold what suffering can afford  
when suffering is not allowed  
to keep the money.

The empire had passed through here  
in velvet and cannon smoke.  
It had taken spice, glass, saints, bodies,  
had renamed the wind, taxed the dawn,  
taught marble to look innocent.

Now its descendants sold magnets  
of the basilica, carnival masks,  
tiny plastic gondolas  
that would never know weight.

I bought nothing.  
I was too tired even for desire.

Near Campo Santa Margherita  
students sat on the pavement  
with cheap wine and black coats,  
their laughter rising like birds  
who had not yet heard of winter.  
One girl sang in a language  
I almost knew.  
Another tuned a cello  
as large and brown as a sleeping animal.

The children ran between them,  
chasing a ball that kept becoming  
the moon, then an orange, then a skull,  
then simply a ball again  
when a man shouted from a window.

Even the surreal grows practical  
after enough hours awake.

A little boy stopped before me  
and asked if I was lost.

I said, I have just arrived.

He considered this.  
Then you are lost, he said,  
and ran back into the square.

Above him, the evening bent down  
to drink from the canal.  
The water swallowed windows, bells,  
the pink afterlife of clouds.  
A boatman pushed his oar  
into the reflection of a palace  
and broke it into coins.

I walked until my feet  
became two small governments  
in open rebellion.

At last I found a room  
under a ceiling crossed by beams  
dark as the ribs of a ship.  
The bed waited with its white accusation.  
But sleep would not come.

Through the wall, someone practiced Bach.  
Through the floor, someone argued about rent.  
Through the shutters, Venice breathed—  
mold, salt, diesel, incense, fish,  
the perfume of money aging badly.

I lay there while the city  
floated inside my skull.  
Marco Polo returned from the east  
with pockets full of impossible animals.  
The winged lion licked its book clean.  
Children built an airport from breadcrumbs.  
Music students stitched the torn lagoon  
with black thread and eighth notes.

And I, citizen of fatigue,  
emigrant from my own body,  
understood nothing except this:

Art is not a palace.  
It is the song leaking  
from the servant’s window.

Empire is not history.  
It is the hand still searching  
your pocket in the dark.

Poverty is not silence.  
It is the violin repeating  
one phrase until the wall remembers.

And exile—  
exile is landing somewhere beautiful  
after a sleepless night,  
hearing children laugh  
among monuments paid for by hunger,  
and feeling, for one trembling second,  
that even the drowned stones  
are trying to go home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that imitates the tone and imagery of a serious contemporary poet: long flowing lines, no rhyme, vivid Venetian details, political undertones, and haunting questions about children, refugees, and history.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk the lagoon lifts its tarnished mirror to the palaces,  
and every window, blind with gold, seems to remember another empire,  
another procession of banners, spices, treaties signed above a table  
while oars knocked softly against the blackened ribs of boats below.  

The water has learned to carry everything without accusation:  
diesel sheen, orange peel, a tourist’s paper map softening at the folds,  
the salt breath of the Adriatic, the names of drowned cities,  
the names of drowned children, which are never written on the tickets.  

In the campo, a boy chases pigeons through the blue hour,  
his shoes flashing like small fish, his laughter striking the stones  
where proclamations once hardened into law, where men in masks  
decided who was foreign, who was useful, who could vanish by morning.  

What does a child know of borders, except the sudden hand at the shoulder,  
the fence appearing where the field had been, the sea changing its mind?  
What does a child know of history, except that adults lower their voices  
when the ships come in, and the news glows all night in the next room?  

Along the Zattere, the moored boats knock and knock,  
as if some old debt were being counted in the dark.  
The church domes float above us, pale as skulls washed clean,  
and the saints look down with their painted wounds, refusing to answer.  

There are men selling umbrellas beneath the arcades,  
men who have crossed deserts with plastic bottles and borrowed names,  
men whose mothers still speak to them in kitchens far from here  
as the rain begins its patient work on marble and cardboard.  

Venice, you elegant survivor, you theater of sinking thresholds,  
how easily you teach the world to admire decay from a balcony.  
We photograph the green bruise of water at the palace steps,  
the gondolier’s striped back, the red flare of an evening spritz,  

and somewhere beyond the breakwater a rubber boat is entering history  
without music, without lanterns, without the blessing of any guide.  
Who will count them when the tide folds its dark ledger closed?  
Who will say the children were more than a number crossing the screen?  

The bells begin again, scattering bronze over the rooftops,  
over laundry, antennas, the secret courtyards full of damp leaves,  
over the lion with its open book, over the locked doors of Europe,  
over the sleeping child whose dream is a country no map can keep.  

And still the water rises, intimate, patient, almost tender,  
touching the stones as if to read what we have carved there:  
victory, commerce, mercy, exclusion, the old magnificent lies.  
What will be left for the children to inherit but this question, shining,  

this city trembling in its beautiful mask,  
this sea that remembers every footstep it has swallowed,  
this silence after the sirens,  
this silence before the next boat appears.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
